transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Owen (Redwood SE), Sara (BlueArc Platform), Tom (BlueArc SRE), Priya (BlueArc ML)

00:00:00 Maya: All right, thanks everyone for hopping on. quick agenda - align success criteria, walk through the harness integration approach, decide streaming vs non-streaming, and lock timeline. Sara, you good with that?
00:00:12 Sara: Yep, that's perfect. Thanks Maya. We got a handful of stakeholders here so I'll keep notes.
00:00:18 Owen: Hi all, I'll try to be pragmatic, show what the adapter looks like and what telemetry we'll produce.
00:00:25 Tom: Quick ask, Tom here, can we keep the window late evening our side? low traffic then.
00:00:29 Maya: Totally, we'll aim for a 4-hr window in your low-traffic slot.

00:01:10 Sara: To set context, BlueArc runs a med-tech triage assistant. We have batched nightly jobs and also call-level inference for triage UI. Our current infra is GCP with a VPC per environment. throughput target is approx 3k reqs/day for now, but we care about peaks - roughly 120 rps burst for 5-10s. Latency SLO for interactive is p95 < 400ms, p99 < 900ms for short prompts (~150 tokens).
00:01:40 Owen: Okay that's helpful. Is the 120rps mostly single-turn short completions or multi-turn chat with KV cache?
00:01:48 Priya: Mostly single-turn but a subset of sessions are multi-turn, might need KV cache support; typical context lengths up to 1k tokens in multi-turn flows.
00:01:58 Maya: For the POC, success criteria you gave (p95/p99) are solid. We'll propose two benchmark profiles: interactive (short prompts, low latency) and batch-stream (nightly jobs, high total throughput but can tolerate higher latency).

00:02:20 Owen: On the harness side, Redwood provides a sample adapter that consumes your client script format. we usually ship a Python harness adapter and a small shim that maps your prompt JSON to the Redwood streaming API or the non-streaming generate endpoint.
00:02:35 Tom: Quick Q on streaming: does streaming change the backend capacity profile a lot? our ops team is worried about tail latency and connection counts.
00:02:45 Owen: It does. Streaming maintains an open connection and amortizes per-token cost differently. With streaming you'll see better perceived latency because tokens start arriving asap, but you also need more connection handling and your client must tolerate partial responses. For capacity, we measure concurrent token emission rates; so a 120rps burst of short prompts is fine with streaming but long multi-turn could tie up sessions.
00:03:10 Sara: If we go streaming for interactive and non-streaming for batch, is that a supported mixed-mode for the POC?
00:03:15 Owen: Yes, fully supported. Redwood runtime can run mixed fleets; the harness can switch endpoints per request type. We'll show the recommended routing policy - interactive -> low-latency nodes, batch -> high-throughput nodes that are quantized.

00:03:40 Priya: For fidelity, we need deterministic token outputs across runs for regression testing. How do you handle model variants and quantization differences?
00:03:49 Owen: Good question. We'll pin a model build id in the POC. we also support side-by-side runs: you can run the same prompt against the unquantized reference and the quantized variant; our harness captures token diffs and a simple quality metric. We'll also export token-level latencies.

00:04:20 Tom: About telemetry - we need per-request traces, token counts, and request body logging disabled by default. SOC2 and audit logs are important for us.
00:04:30 Maya: We'll share the security checklist—SAML SSO, KMS integration, and audit log retention options. For the POC we can run with masked logs; full payload logging is opt-in after legal signs off.

00:05:05 Sara: Great. Let's talk about workload synthesis: we have customer scripts in a bespoke JSON format. do you adapt or do we need to convert?
00:05:12 Owen: We can adapt. The adapter will parse your JSON and emit the proper streaming frames or non-stream RPCs. Ideally you send a small sample of your script format - about 10-20 representative templates - and we'll map them.
00:05:27 Sara: We'll send three templates first, then a larger set.

00:05:45 Owen: For load generation, Redwood recommends two harness modes: a client-side generator that mimics real arrival patterns (burstiness, think peaks), and a server-side load generator we've used for very high qps. For the POC we'll likely use your client script runner with our shim, because that exercises end-to-end path and mirrors production logic.
00:06:05 Maya: On acceptance criteria, let's make them explicit: 1) Interactive profile - p95 < 400ms, p99 < 900ms for 150-token prompts for 30m sustained with occasional 120rps bursts. 2) Batch profile - sustain overall throughput of X tokens/sec equivalent with 99% success rate for 2-hr window. 3) Quality - no more than 2% generation regressions vs reference. 4) Observability - per-request traces and token-level telemetry available. Agree?
00:06:35 Sara: I'm fine, but need to confirm the exact tokens/sec for batch - Priya will give that number.
00:06:41 Priya: We're targeting about 20k tokens/minute for the nightly job; I'll confirm exact qps.

00:07:05 Tom: Networking: we'll need a peering or a temporary ingress allowlist. our preference is VPC peering to avoid public endpoints. any constraints on IP ranges?
00:07:13 Owen: We'll operate through our private deployment option for the POC (customer-managed VPC peering). We just need your subnet and egress rules; we'll provide a small EC2/GCE-side test harness if peering is slow to set up.
00:07:30 Sara: Any special storage required for KV cache warmup? we sometimes preload conversation context into cache for warm start.
00:07:36 Owen: We support KV cache warmup via the harness; it's just a set of warmup calls that populate the server-side cache. we can script that. we'll include warmup steps in the runbook.

00:08:10 Maya: timeline proposal: send workload matrix and adapter by next week, internal bluearc to confirm prompts and peering by 2026-07-11, schedule the live benchmark window around 2026-07-14, results and retrospective by 2026-07-20. Does that map to your timelines?
00:08:28 Sara: sounds good, we might need a day buffer but okay.

00:09:00 Owen: Small note on measurement: we'll record cold-starts and steady-state. cold-start defined as new model shard or empty KV cache; tail latency measurements will include cold-start buckets so you can see where spikes come from.
00:09:15 Priya: good, we want the breakdown. And can you provide token cost estimates per model variant?
00:09:22 Maya: yes we will include cost per 1M tokens for the referenced configs and an estimate for the POC run.

00:09:50 Tom: Regarding security docs - we need to confirm whether Redwood's private deployment uses our KMS or Redwood-managed keys.
00:09:58 Owen: For private deployment you can bring-your-own-KMS/HSM. for hosted POC we can also encrypt at rest with customer keys via KMS integration. We'll send the KMS integration notes.

00:10:20 Sara: Any limitations on client languages for the adapter? we're Python heavy but have some Node services.
00:10:26 Owen: We'll provide Python and a minimal Node example; the adapter is tiny - a mapping layer plus the stream handling.

00:10:45 Maya: I want to call out a risk - if the customer scripts rely on specific tokenization or post-processing logic, those need to be included in the harness to make apples-to-apples quality comparisons.
00:10:58 Priya: good call, we do custom postprocessing. I'll package that with the prompt templates.

00:11:20 Sara: Regarding metrics - what dashboards do you provide?
00:11:25 Owen: Redwood Console will provide per-route p50/p95/p99, token breakdown, request traces. We'll share access to a temporary dashboard during the POC.

00:12:00 Maya: let's talk about failure modes - our automatic fallbacks can route to a cheaper quantized variant under load. do you want that enabled for the POC?
00:12:11 Priya: for the POC we want baseline results first, so no auto-fallbacks during acceptance runs. after the run we can test fallback behavior.
00:12:20 Maya: Agreed. We'll run acceptance with fixed routing and then run a resilience test with fallback toggled on.

00:13:00 Tom: Are there any special compliance checks for healthcare data? we mostly redacted PHI, but still: audit trails, retention settings?
00:13:09 Maya: We'll supply our compliance pack which covers SOC2 + incremental addenda for healthcare, plus guidance on data retention and redaction. For POC we'll only send hashed or synthetic data.

00:13:40 Sara: Ok last item - who's the main contact for day-of run?
00:13:44 Maya: Maya will be AE lead, Owen will run the harness and be the SE lead. Sara and Tom will be BlueArc day-of contacts.

00:14:00 Owen: I'll demo the adapter now quickly - show a tiny snippet. (demo noise)
00:14:18 Owen: Example: you map your JSON prompt to a call like generate(stream=True) and the shim attaches metadata headers (customer-id, txn-id) so we correlate traces. The harness emits traces to Jaeger and metrics to Prometheus.
00:14:40 Priya: Jaeger + Prom is perfect. do you also export to cloud-native telemetry?
00:14:45 Owen: yes we can forward metrics to your cloud monitoring.

00:15:05 Sara: Any gotchas with token counting? our billing team needs consistent token math.
00:15:12 Owen: Tokenization differences can cause small diffs. We'll include a tokenizer module used during the POC so both sides use the same token counts.

00:15:35 Maya: wrap-up - owners and dates in the action items. we'll send the workload matrix and the draft POC runbook within two business days.
00:15:45 Sara: thanks all, this is good.

00:16:00 (meeting threads + some small cross talk as people drop)

Recap (auto):
- Goal: Validate interactive latency and nightly throughput with customer scripts; measure quality vs reference.
- Deliverables: adapter, workload matrix, runbook, security docs, live bench window.
- Acceptance: explicit p95/p99 targets, quality regression threshold, telemetry availability.
